title: A Song for the Sabbath Day
superscription: A Psalm. A song for the Sabbath day.

verses.text: It is good to praise the LORD, and to sing praises to Your name, O Most High,
to proclaim Your loving devotion in the morning and Your faithfulness at night
with the ten-stringed harp and the melody of the lyre.
For You, O LORD, have made me glad by Your deeds; I sing for joy at the works of Your hands.
How great are Your works, O LORD, how deep are Your thoughts!
A senseless man does not know, and a fool does not understand,
that though the wicked sprout like grass, and all evildoers flourish, they will be forever destroyed.
But You, O LORD, are exalted forever!
For surely Your enemies, O LORD, surely Your enemies will perish; all evildoers will be scattered.
But You have exalted my horn like that of a wild ox; with fine oil I have been anointed.
My eyes see the downfall of my enemies; my ears hear the wailing of my wicked foes.
The righteous will flourish like a palm tree, and grow like a cedar in Lebanon.
Planted in the house of the LORD, they will flourish in the courts of our God.
In old age they will still bear fruit; healthy and green they will remain,
to proclaim, "The LORD is upright; He is my Rock, and in Him there is no unrighteousness."

context.author: Not named. Book Four (Psalms 90-106) opens with “a prayer of Moses,” and most of its psalms have no title. The Greek Old Testament gives several of them to David, and Hebrews 4:7 quotes Psalm 95 as spoken “through David.”
context.genre: Psalm: a song or prayer in Hebrew poetry
context.audience: Israel at worship, and the nations called to join
context.setting: The title calls it “A song for the Sabbath day.” “It is good to praise the LORD, and to sing praises to Your name, O Most High, to proclaim Your loving devotion in the morning and Your faithfulness at night” (vv.1-2), with harp and lyre (v.3). “How great are Your works, O LORD, how deep are Your thoughts!” (v.5). The fool does not see that the wicked “sprout like grass” only to be destroyed (vv.6-7), while the LORD is exalted forever (v.8). God has made the singer strong like a wild ox and anointed him (v.10). “The righteous will flourish like a palm tree, and grow like a cedar in Lebanon. Planted in the house of the LORD, they will flourish in the courts of our God. In old age they will still bear fruit” (vv.12-14), to proclaim, “The LORD is upright; He is my Rock” (v.15).
context.custom: The Mishnah says the Levites sang this psalm in the Temple on the Sabbath, with a set psalm for each day of the week (Tamid 7:4). Date palms grow tall and straight and bear fruit for many decades; cedars of Lebanon live for centuries. David pictured himself as “an olive tree flourishing in the house of God” (Psalm 52:8).
context.timelineImmediate: Psalm 93 begins the songs that proclaim, ‘The LORD reigns!’
context.timelineBible: Jesus said, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27), and Hebrews speaks of “a Sabbath rest for the people of God” (Hebrews 4:9). Jesus taught that every good tree bears good fruit (Matthew 7:17), and Paul prayed that believers would be “filled with the fruit of righteousness” (Philippians 1:11).

translation.meaning: Date palm; also the name Tamar.
Cedar, the great tree of Lebanon.

gospelParallels.note: Abide in Me and bear much fruit.

otBackground.note: Like a tree planted by streams.
Like a tree planted by the waters.

overview.summary: A Sabbath song: it is good to praise God morning and night; the wicked sprout like grass and wither, but the righteous, planted in God’s house, flourish like palm and cedar and bear fruit into old age.
overview.settingLine: Praise morning and night on the day of rest.

history.t: Levites sang a psalm for each day.
Given at creation and at Sinai.

customs.t: A psalm sung for each day of the week.

archaeology.t: Harps and lyres with many strings appear on Assyrian and Egyptian reliefs.
A 2,000-year-old date seed from Masada was grown into a living palm.

overview.discussion: The righteous “still bear fruit” in old age (v.14). What fruit do I hope my life will still bear at the end?
overview.book: The book of Psalms · 150 psalms (1-100 in the app so far). Israel’s songs and prayers: praise, lament, thanks, trust and wisdom, many of them by David.
overview.author: Not named
